newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia utility revamp won't spark aluminium sector.
newsitem.headline: Russia utility revamp won't spark aluminium sector.

text.p: Russian government efforts to drive down electricity bills for industrial users are unlikely to help the bulk of the country's power-guzzling aluminium smelters, metals analysts said on Wednesday.
"Electricity costs could affect production, but they are unlikely to do so substantially," said Boris Arlyuk, St Petersburg, Russia-based analyst for Brook Hunt International.
Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin on Wednesday announced a government plan to split national electricity monopoly UES's distribution arm from the rest of the company.
UES, or Unified Energy System, owns 29 power plants, holds stakes in all but two of Russia's 72 "energo" regional utilities and is one of Russia's biggest companies by market capitalisation.
It is struggling for control over Irkutskenergo, which supplies the big Irkutsk aluminium smelter in southern Siberia.

Yasin said restructuring would introduce competition to Russia's power supply and distribution system by allowing individual power plants to offer electricity to industrial enterprises on a competitive price basis.
"Russian production costs are on average higher than world levels but below world market prices of aluminium today," said Anthony Bird of Anthony Bird Associates in London.
The price of electricity -- a major cost in producing aluminium -- is the not the only problem for Russia's aluminium industry, which accounts for about 15 percent of world output.

"Electricity costs are not a huge killer for them (Siberian aluminium smelters) compared to, say, transportation costs, which can be crippling," said Peter Houlder, managing director of CentreInvest Consultancy in Moscow.
The four biggest smelters in Russia are based in Siberia, where power generated by mighty rivers is cheap and plentiful.
Siberian smelters accounted for about three quarters of Russian primary aluminium output of 2.87 million tonnes in 1996.
One analyst said competition in the electricity supply business could even scupper smelters' plans to sign long-term, cheap electricity supply deals, and leave them paying more.

"I think splitting off the distribution arm could simplify cross-subsidy issues and make trade-offs explicit which are currently implicit," he said, referring to the cheap energy supply deals Russian smelters are racing to negotiate.
But smaller plants in the Urals and the European part of Russia could benefit from competitively-priced electricity because they already pay more than their Siberian cousins.
Analysts said Russian smelters, encouraged by stronger world aluminium prices, might for now be less obsessed with whether their energy supplies will get cheaper.
Benchmark three-month aluminium prices on the London Metal Exchange were at around $1,625 late on Wednesday, well above the last low of $1,305 in October 1996.

Arlyuk estimated that even with LME prices of $1,500, the four Siberian smelters -- Bratsk, Krasnoyarsk, Sayansk and Irkutsk -- were operating at a gross profit of between $150 and $220 per tonne of metal delivered to Rotterdam.
Smelters in the European part of Russia were making losses of between $40 and $80 on the same basis, he said.

Still, cheaper electricity won't solve the Russian aluminium industry's long term problems of modernisation, securing raw materials supplies, attracting foreign investment and transporting material across half the globe to buyers.
"The combined costs of electricity and freight rates are absolutely crucial (in the long term)," said Bird.
